questions.stem: The task below tests this skill. Given house values [12, 5, 8, 9, 10], what is the maximum sum obtainable by choosing non-adjacent houses?

options.misconception: subtracts a value as if one house had to be removed
takes only the single largest value
adds every house and ignores the adjacency constraint

questions.explanation: At each house the optimal value is the max of taking it plus the best up to two houses back, versus skipping it; evaluating that recurrence gives 30. Summing all values violates the no-adjacent rule.
questions.hint: Keep two running bests: best ending at the previous house and best ending two houses back.

questions.stem: Compute the result for this case. When F(n) with F(0)=0, F(1)=1 is computed by recursive memoization, how many distinct subproblem values F(k) are ever computed, for k from 0 up to n = 7?

omits both base cases from the state count

questions.stem: The item below needs a solution. Union-find over elements 0..5 starts with each element its own component. After unions (0,0), (3,3), (5,1), how many components remain?

options.misconception: subtracts one per union without checking whether endpoints were already connected

adds one from miscounting the initial number of components

questions.stem: Reason carefully about this case. A Bloom filter has m = 13 bits and hash functions h1(x)=x mod m, h2(x)=(2x+1) mod m. Which bit positions are set when key 40 is inserted?

swaps the two hash formulas
adds two to each hashed position

questions.explanation: Computing h1(40) and h2(40) gives bit positions 1, 3. Both functions must be applied; using only one or shifting the formulas sets the wrong bits and can create false negatives if checked inconsistently.

questions.stem: Work from the stated assumptions. What is the expected time to search for an element in a skip list of n items with geometric promotion?

assumes direct addressing without any traversal
treats the express lanes as if they did not skip nodes

questions.explanation: O(log n) follows from the geometric distribution of tower heights: with promotion probability 1/2 the expected tower height is 2, and the express lanes give logarithmic expected search time. Assuming no promotion or a linear scan ignores the skipping structure.
questions.hint: Think of the geometric series for tower heights and how express lanes shorten the path.

questions.stem: Work through the problem below. For a sorted array of n = 127 elements, how many key comparisons does binary search make in the worst case?

options.misconception: doubles the depth instead of recognizing that each step halves the interval
off by one below the tree depth by forgetting the root comparison
off by one above the depth by counting the empty final interval

questions.explanation: A binary search over n = 2^7 - 1 elements builds a complete decision tree of height 6, so the deepest leaf needs 7 comparisons; each comparison halves the remaining range, which is why the count is logarithmic and not linear.
questions.hint: Write n + 1 as a power of two; the number of comparisons is that exponent.

questions.stem: Apply the concept to this instance. For the recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n^2, what is the tight asymptotic bound of T(n)?

options.misconception: applies the case-2 log factor even when f(n) is not Θ(n^{log_b a})
assumes the recursion always collapses to a single linear pass
takes only the trivial bound and ignores both recursive work and f(n)

questions.explanation: Here log base 2 of 2 equals 1, so the recursive work is Θ(n^1); comparing that exponent with the 2 in f(n) selects the Master Theorem case that yields Θ(n^2).

questions.subject: DATA_STRUCTURES
questions.stem: Examine the case described here. A dynamic array starts with capacity 16 and doubles its capacity whenever it is full. After 47 append operations, how many element copies have occurred in total?

options.misconception: assumes exactly one resize of the initial capacity occurs
overestimates by imagining a copy on every append
counts only the m insertions and ignores every resize copy

questions.explanation: Resizes happen when size reaches capacity; the copied amounts are 16, 32, and so on up to the last resize, summing to 48. Because each element is copied at most once per doubling level, the total is below 2m, giving amortized O(1) per append.
questions.hint: Track size and capacity together; a resize copies the current size, then capacity doubles.

questions.stem: The following case is given. For an input of size n = 3525, what is the worst-case auxiliary space (excluding the input) used by merge sort on an array?

options.misconception: assumes no call stack or auxiliary buffer is ever allocated
confuses the depth of a balanced recursion with a linear stack
mixes the time bound of a sort into its space bound

questions.explanation: Auxiliary space counts extra memory beyond the input. For merge sort on an array the dominant extra allocation grows as O(n); call-stack frames or a temporary buffer scale with that quantity, and this measure is distinct from the algorithm's running time.
questions.hint: Separate time from space: ask how deep the recursion goes or how large the extra buffer is.

leaves the list unchanged because the new node was never linked in
inserts the new value twice instead of once

questions.learningObjective: demonstrate understanding of doubly linked lists
questions.stem: A typical exam item asks this: A doubly linked list holds 18 <-> 15 <-> 21 <-> 24 <-> 6 <-> 12. The node with value 6 is deleted and its prev/next links are repaired. What remains?

options.misconception: drops an extra node by breaking the head link
forgets to relink the neighbors and leaves the removed node in place
moves the node to the tail instead of deleting it

questions.explanation: Deletion sets the successor's prev pointer to the predecessor and the predecessor's next pointer to the successor, bypassing the node of value 6. The result is 18 <-> 15 <-> 21 <-> 24 <-> 12; failing to update both directions is the classic bug.
questions.hint: A doubly linked deletion must patch both prev and next of the surrounding nodes.
